opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I worked on GATE, so some of these are criticisms of my own choices. The main concern is that the way GATE handles software is quite stylized. In the model, algorithmic progress is essentially a multiplier on effective compute, and the speed of that progress depends on how much you invest in it, with some diminishing returns. That's a reasonable first approximation, but it hides a lot of what actually matters.

The biggest issue for me is how software R&D interacts with compute. In practice, almost all frontier algorithmic progress comes from running experiments, and experiments need compute. So the idea that you can scale up software progress by throwing more researchers at the problem, or eventually more AI researchers, runs into the fact that the experimental compute budget is a hard input. If you model software R&D as mostly labor-driven, you get much more explosive dynamics once AI automates that labor. That's the core of the "software-only intelligence explosion" story, and I think it's overstated. GATE doesn't fully resolve this, but I'd want any model to be very explicit about the complementarity between cognitive labor and compute in R&D. My view is that the substitutability is fairly low, so compute bottlenecks bind hard.

A second concern is treating "progress toward AGI" as a single scalar, effective compute, where you cross a threshold and get full automation. Real capabilities are lumpy. Software progress might make models much better at things that are easy to benchmark, like coding puzzles and math competitions, while leaving gaps in agency, long-horizon planning, robustness, and messy real-world tasks. Collapsing all of that into one number that maps onto a fraction of tasks automated is convenient, but it can make you think you're closer than you are, because benchmarked progress looks impressive.

Third, the parameters are poorly constrained. We have some estimates of historical algorithmic efficiency gains, things like halving the compute needed for a given performance every eight months or so, but those come from narrow domains and noisy measurements. Extrapolating them, and especially extrapolating how they respond to massive increases in investment, involves a lot of guesswork. Small changes in the returns-to-research parameter can flip you between slow, steady progress and a near singularity. So I'd treat the model's outputs as illustrations of what follows from certain assumptions, not as forecasts.

On net I think GATE gets the macro picture roughly right. The big driver is scaling compute and investment, with AI automating more of the economy over time. But I'd be skeptical of anyone who uses the software R&D part of the model to argue for very fast takeoff timelines, because that's exactly where the model is weakest.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic progress depends on investment and that experiments need compute, but it does not state that software efficiency gains vary with the compute used to train a model.

r002.rationale: It questions whether benchmark gains in coding and math reflect broader AGI progress, but does not address progress measured in computer vision and language modeling at current capability levels.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute bottlenecks and software R&D’s effects on takeoff dynamics, but does not say that removing software R&D has the same effect as increasing AGI training compute requirements.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I was one of the people who worked on GATE, so these are concerns I have about my own work as much as anything. But I think the biggest one is that the model basically treats software R&D as this one-dimensional thing. You have a software stock, you put in researcher labor and compute for experiments, and that turns into more effective compute. And the way AI feeds back into that is just, AI substitutes for the human researcher labor in that production function.

The problem is that this abstracts away almost everything that's actually hard about getting to AGI. In the real world, when a lab does software R&D, they're not just dialing up a single scalar. They're figuring out how to get models to do long-horizon tasks, how to get them to learn on the job, how to get them to be reliable in agentic settings, all these things that are qualitatively different capabilities. And the model just doesn't have a representation of that. It has a notion of effective compute, and then there's a mapping from effective compute to how much of the economy's tasks you can automate, and that mapping is sort of assumed rather than derived from anything.

So one worry is that we're probably overstating how smooth the path is. If there are specific capabilities that current approaches just don't get you, and you need some conceptual breakthrough that doesn't come from having more labor thrown at the problem, the model won't see that. It'll just say, well, you have ten times more researchers now, so you get this much more progress.

The second concern, which is sort of the flip side, is about the substitution between compute and labor in R&D. The model lets you trade these off, and the elasticity there matters enormously for whether you get a software-only intelligence explosion or not. And I just don't think we have good evidence about that parameter. My own intuition is that experiments are a much bigger bottleneck than the model's default parameters imply. If you look at what researchers at frontier labs actually spend their time on, a lot of it is waiting for runs to finish, and having a million AI researchers doesn't help you much if they're all competing for the same cluster. The model can represent that, but whether you get an explosion or not is really sensitive to how you set it, and I think people reading the headline results don't always appreciate how much is riding on an assumption rather than on data.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more philosophical, is that the model has this notion that there's some finite amount of software progress between here and full automation. Like, there's a target you're moving toward. And I'm not sure that's the right framing. It might be that the thing that matters isn't the algorithms at all, it's the deployment, the learning from being embedded in the economy, the data you get from actually doing the tasks. And if that's true, then software R&D in the lab is just not the variable you want to be tracking. So I'd say the model is useful for thinking about the compute side, about how investment scales, about the economics. But I'd be pretty cautious about reading the software R&D part as telling you much about when AGI arrives.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether modeled software progress translates smoothly to AGI, but does not address progress in computer vision and language modeling at current capability levels.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that removing software R&D contributions from GATE has the same effect as raising AGI training compute requirements.

astra-6.text:
My main concern is that software R&D is doing a lot of work in the model, but we don’t really know how to translate improvements in software into progress toward AGI. You can measure an improvement on a particular task, or how much less compute you need to reach a particular level of performance. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you how much closer you are to a system that can automate research across the board.

For example, an algorithmic improvement might make training twice as efficient. That’s valuable, but is it equivalent to having twice as much compute for every capability we care about? Does it help with long-horizon planning or with identifying promising research directions? That depends on the improvement. If you compress all of this into a single measure of software progress, those distinctions can disappear.

And that becomes especially important when you close the feedback loop: better AI produces more software research, which produces better AI. The strength of that feedback depends on whether the research is actually improving the capabilities that are bottlenecking further automation. Increasing the volume of research isn’t necessarily the same as resolving those bottlenecks.

So I think it’s useful to explore that mechanism in a model. But I’d be cautious about interpreting the resulting trajectory as a robust prediction. A lot depends on assumptions about the composition and transferability of software improvements that we have relatively little evidence about.

r001.rationale: The response gives an example of training becoming twice as efficient, but does not state that efficiency gains vary depending on how much compute is used.

r002.rationale: It questions how software improvements translate to broad research automation, but does not specifically discuss progress measured in computer vision and language modeling at current capability levels or compare its rate to AGI progress.

r003.rationale: It discusses software R&D’s role in the feedback loop, but does not say that removing those contributions has the same effect as increasing AGI’s training compute requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
My main concern is that software R&D is doing a lot of work in the model, but it’s quite difficult to say what the relevant output actually is. If you improve an algorithm so that you can achieve the same performance with less compute, that’s a fairly clear kind of progress. But progress toward AGI also involves developing capabilities that you didn’t have before, and it’s not obvious that those two things can be represented by a single quantity.

For example, you might get much better at training the kinds of models we already know how to train without resolving whatever limitations prevent them from doing autonomous research. If you represent all software progress as a general efficiency improvement, you risk assuming that those limitations disappear as you accumulate enough of it.

That matters especially for the feedback loop. AI helps with software research, software research improves AI, and then the improved AI does more research. That’s a plausible mechanism, but how strong it is depends on which research tasks the AI can actually do and whether those tasks are the bottleneck. I’d want to be cautious about treating the resulting trajectory as a prediction when some of the most consequential assumptions are built into how we represent progress in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response mentions achieving the same performance with less compute, but does not say that software efficiency gains vary with the amount of compute used to train a model.

r002.rationale: It questions whether improvements to existing models remove limitations to AGI, but does not specifically compare progress in computer vision and language modeling at current capability levels with AGI progress at the same rate.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that removing software R&D contributions from GATE has the same effect as increasing AGI training compute requirements.
